props.title: PixiJS — 2D WebGL & WebGPU Creation Engine
props.subtitle: High-performance hardware-accelerated 2D graphics, scene graphs, and batch rendering

what.definition: PixiJS is a rendering engine that allows you to create rich, interactive 2D graphics, cross-platform applications, and games using WebGL and WebGPU without dealing with complex lower-level shader code.
what.summary: A battle-tested 2D rendering library that provides a hierarchical scene graph, automatic draw-call batching, multi-texture optimization, custom filters, and asset management for 60+ FPS web graphics.
bullets: Hierarchical Scene Graph: Tree structure with Containers, Sprites, Graphics, and Text
Automatic Batch Rendering: Bundles thousands of draw calls into single GPU passes
WebGL & WebGPU Dual Backends: Modern hardware acceleration with automatic fallbacks
Asset Management & Texture Atlases: Asynchronous loading, caching, and sprite sheet slicing

why.summary: Raw HTML5 2D Canvas struggles when animating thousands of objects due to CPU rasterization bottlenecks, while raw WebGL requires hundreds of lines of shader setup and matrix math boilerplate.
why.impact: PixiJS bridges this gap by offering a clean, intuitive display tree API while unlocking the full speed of the GPU, powering interactive maps, data visualizations, and production web games at locked 60 FPS.

terms.shortDefinition: The main convenience wrapper that initializes the Renderer, Ticker, and root Stage Container.
terms.detailedDefinition: PIXI.Application encapsulates canvas DOM creation, requestAnimationFrame loop management via Ticker, and sets up the root stage container. It provides a simple start point for interactive 2D projects.
terms.whyItMatters: Eliminates hundreds of lines of boilerplate setup for WebGL canvas context creation, screen resizing, and animation frame hooks.

dialogue.user: How do I spin up a new PixiJS canvas?
dialogue.aiThoughts: User needs the standard entry point object.
dialogue.aiQuestion: Instantiate `const app = new PIXI.Application(); await app.init({ width: 800, height: 600 }); document.body.appendChild(app.canvas);`

terms.shortDefinition: A general display node that holds a collection of children and propagates position, rotation, and scale down the hierarchy.
terms.detailedDefinition: Containers do not render pixels directly; instead, they manage hierarchical spatial transformations. When a container moves, rotates, or scales, all its children inherit those transforms via world matrix multiplication.
terms.whyItMatters: Allows complex composite game objects (like a character with separate body, weapon, and shadow sprites) to be moved and transformed as a single unit.

dialogue.user: How do I move a group of 20 sprites together?
dialogue.aiThoughts: Group them under a single parent display node.
dialogue.aiQuestion: Add them to a `PIXI.Container` and update only the container's `x` and `y` properties!

terms.shortDefinition: The fundamental 2D display object that renders a textured quad onto the screen.
terms.detailedDefinition: A Sprite binds a source Texture (or a sub-region of a texture atlas) to rectangular geometry. It supports anchors, pivot points, alpha transparency, tint colors, and blend modes.
terms.whyItMatters: Sprites are the core building block for 90% of visual elements in 2D games and dashboards, and are heavily optimized by Pixi's batch renderer.

dialogue.user: What is the difference between a Texture and a Sprite?
dialogue.aiThoughts: Differentiate the GPU asset from the scene graph display object.
dialogue.aiQuestion: A Texture is the raw image data on the GPU; a Sprite is the visible instance in the scene tree with position, scale, and tint.

terms.shortDefinition: An object representing an image resource or frame stored in WebGL GPU video memory.
terms.detailedDefinition: Textures wrap a BaseTexture (the actual GPU texture buffer) with UV coordinate frames. Multiple Textures can share a single BaseTexture (such as sprites in a texture atlas / spritesheet).
terms.whyItMatters: Sharing a single BaseTexture across multiple sprites allows the BatchRenderer to draw them in a single draw call without expensive GPU texture bind swaps.

dialogue.user: Why should I use a spritesheet instead of separate PNG files?
dialogue.aiQuestion: Because all sprites referencing the same spritesheet share one BaseTexture, allowing PixiJS to render thousands of sprites in 1 GPU draw call.

terms.shortDefinition: An internal rendering system that combines multiple textured quads into a single WebGL drawArrays/drawElements call.
terms.detailedDefinition: Instead of executing one draw call per sprite, BatchRenderer buffers sprite vertices, UVs, tints, and multi-texture indices into dynamic vertex buffers, flushing to the GPU only when texture limits or blend mode changes require a batch break.
terms.whyItMatters: Draw calls are the primary performance bottleneck in WebGL; batching allows PixiJS to render 10,000+ moving sprites at 60 FPS on modest mobile hardware.

dialogue.user: What causes a 'batch break' that degrades performance?
dialogue.aiThoughts: Identify state changes that force a flush.
dialogue.aiQuestion: Switching to an unbound texture, changing blend modes, or interleaving custom shaders breaks the current batch and forces a new draw call.

terms.shortDefinition: A high-precision animation loop manager driven by window.requestAnimationFrame.
terms.detailedDefinition: The Ticker dispatches update events every frame with delta time multipliers. It automatically manages frame-rate throttling, pause when tabs are inactive, and priority queues for update listeners.
terms.whyItMatters: Ensures smooth, delta-compensated physics and animations that run consistently regardless of device refresh rate (60Hz, 120Hz, 144Hz).

dialogue.user: How do I animate a rotating sprite smoothly?
dialogue.aiThoughts: Connect to ticker callback with deltaTime.
dialogue.aiQuestion: Attach a callback to `app.ticker.add((time) => { sprite.rotation += 0.05 * time.deltaTime; })`

terms.shortDefinition: A fast, streamlined container designed to render massive numbers of simple sprites with minimal CPU overhead.
terms.detailedDefinition: ParticleContainer trades advanced features (such as deep nesting, masks, filters, and per-child rotation/tint when disabled) for ultra-fast GPU streaming, uploading flat vertex buffers directly to the shader.
terms.whyItMatters: Can render 50,000+ particles (snow, rain, bullets, starfields) at 60 FPS where standard Containers would suffer CPU transform overhead.

dialogue.user: When should I use ParticleContainer instead of Container?
dialogue.aiThoughts: Determine when raw particle volume trumps hierarchy features.
dialogue.aiQuestion: Use ParticleContainer for massive flat particle systems (bullets, explosions, rain) where children don't need complex sub-nesting or filters.

terms.shortDefinition: A post-processing effect applied via custom GLSL fragment and vertex shaders.
terms.detailedDefinition: Filters render a display object into a temporary offscreen framebuffer (render texture), then apply shader passes (e.g. Blur, ColorMatrix, Glow, Displacement) before compositing the result back to the screen.
terms.whyItMatters: Unlocks AAA visual effects like water distortion, bloom, drop shadows, and color grading directly inside the browser.

dialogue.user: Why does applying many filters slow down my frame rate?
dialogue.aiQuestion: Each filter requires switching render targets to offscreen framebuffers, which increases GPU memory bandwidth and interrupts sprite batching.

questions.question: What is the structural difference between a 'Texture' and a 'BaseTexture' in PixiJS?

choices.text: Texture is for 3D meshes; BaseTexture is for 2D sprites
choices.explanation: PixiJS is a 2D rendering engine; both handle 2D image data.

choices.text: BaseTexture holds the actual raw WebGL GPU image resource, while Texture defines a specific UV rectangular crop of that BaseTexture
choices.explanation: BaseTexture owns the GPU memory allocation. Multiple Texture instances can reference sub-regions (UV frames) of the same BaseTexture, enabling sprite sheets.

choices.text: BaseTexture is rendered by CPU, whereas Texture is rendered by GPU
choices.explanation: Both are part of the GPU texture management system.

choices.text: They are identical aliases with no technical distinction
choices.explanation: They have distinct responsibilities: GPU resource vs UV sub-region definition.

questions.hint: Think about how a sprite sheet texture atlas shares one large image across dozens of sprite frames.

questions.question: How does the 'Ticker' deltaTime property help maintain consistent movement speed across different monitor refresh rates (60Hz vs 144Hz)?

choices.text: It forces all monitors to run at exactly 60 FPS by sleeping the thread
choices.explanation: Ticker does not sleep the main JS thread; it measures actual elapsed time.

choices.text: It provides a frame duration multiplier proportional to 60 FPS, scaling velocity so distance per second remains identical
choices.explanation: At 60 FPS, deltaTime is ~1.0. At 120 FPS, deltaTime is ~0.5. Multiplying velocity by deltaTime ensures identical movement speed in physical time.

choices.text: It skips rendering every second frame on high-refresh monitors
choices.explanation: PixiJS renders on every RAF frame to deliver maximum visual smoothness.

choices.text: It converts pixel measurements to meters automatically
choices.explanation: Pixel measurements are preserved; deltaTime scales numerical step changes.

questions.hint: Consider what multiplier is needed when a frame executes in 8.3ms (120Hz) instead of 16.6ms (60Hz).

categories.title: Display Objects & Scene Graph
categories.subtitle: Hierarchical visual tree structure
categories.description: The core nodes used to organize, position, and render visual content in PixiJS.
categories.details: Containers provide hierarchical spatial transforms (x, y, scale, rotation, skew) and alpha blending. Sprites bind 2D textures to quads. AnimatedSprite cycles frame sequences, and NineSliceSprite preserves borders during UI resizing.
categories.analogy: Like a Photoshop layer hierarchy where moving a group folder automatically moves all sub-layers inside it.
categories.primaryFocus: Organizing game worlds, UI panels, and multi-part character puppets.
inScope: Local vs World coordinate space conversion
outOfScope: Physics simulation (delegate to Matter.js or Rapier)

categories.title: Vector Graphics & Geometry
categories.subtitle: Procedural shapes, paths, and meshes
categories.description: Dynamic shape drawing and custom vertex mesh manipulation on the GPU.
categories.details: Graphics generates 2D vector shapes (rectangles, circles, bezier paths, polygons) converted on-the-fly into triangulated vertex buffers. MeshSimple and MeshRope allow deformable ribbons, flags, and custom geometry.
categories.analogy: Like an SVG vector canvas with stroke and fill commands, but compiled into GPU triangle primitives.
categories.primaryFocus: Drawing debug bounds, dynamic UI wireframes, health bars, and deformable rope ribbons.

categories.title: Typography & Text Rendering
categories.subtitle: Canvas text vs GPU bitmap fonts
categories.description: Text display strategies balancing styling flexibility against 60 FPS render performance.
categories.details: PIXI.Text rasterizes fonts using HTML5 2D Canvas context and generates an internal texture. PIXI.BitmapText renders characters from pre-baked XML/JSON font atlases using batched quads for zero CPU overhead.
categories.analogy: PIXI.Text is like printing a new photo each time words change; BitmapText is like stamping pre-carved wooden letter blocks.
categories.primaryFocus: Rendering dialog boxes, score counters, HUD indicators, and localized strings.
inScope: PIXI.Text with styling (drop shadow, gradient fill, stroke)
PIXI.BitmapText with high-speed batched character quads
HTMLText for rich HTML/CSS formatted labels
outOfScope: Complex RTL bidirectional text shaping without plugins

categories.title: Shaders, Filters & Post-Processing
categories.subtitle: Custom GLSL effects and full-screen passes
categories.description: GPU fragment and vertex shader pipelines for lighting, blur, distortion, and stylization.
categories.details: Filters render target objects into offscreen framebuffers and pass them through custom GLSL shaders. ColorMatrixFilter provides tinting/grayscale, BlurFilter softens edges, and DisplacementFilter creates liquid ripples.
categories.analogy: Like applying real-time Instagram filters and optical lenses over rendered canvas layers.
categories.primaryFocus: Visual juice: shockwaves, water reflections, CRT monitors, glow highlights, and color grading.
inScope: Custom GLSL fragment and vertex shader filters

categories.title: High-Performance Batching & Particles
categories.subtitle: Ultra-high-throughput rendering pipelines
categories.description: Techniques for rendering tens of thousands of simultaneous entities at locked 60 FPS.
categories.details: ParticleContainer strips complex scene-graph overhead to pump raw vertex buffers directly to the GPU. Texture atlases group assets into single BaseTextures to avoid draw-call batch breaks.
categories.analogy: Like a freight train loading thousands of identical shipping crates at once rather than sending individual courier trucks.
categories.primaryFocus: Bullet hell shoot-em-ups, weather effects (snow/rain), particle explosions, and massive starfields.
inScope: ParticleContainer with selective dynamic properties (position, scale, uv)
Spritesheet atlas packaging to eliminate batch breaks
Object pooling to avoid GC pauses
outOfScope: Complex nested hierarchy inside particle containers

questions.question: When should you prefer PIXI.ParticleContainer over a standard PIXI.Container?

choices.text: When you need deeply nested hierarchy trees and individual child blur filters
choices.explanation: ParticleContainer does not support deep nesting or individual child filters.

choices.text: When you need to render thousands of flat, high-speed sprites (e.g. bullets, rain, snow) with minimal CPU overhead
choices.explanation: ParticleContainer streams flat vertex buffers directly to the GPU shader, bypassing full scene-graph matrix recalculations.

choices.text: When you are rendering static vector SVG shapes
choices.explanation: ParticleContainer is designed exclusively for textured sprite quads.

choices.text: When you want to display HTML form inputs
choices.explanation: HTML inputs are managed in the DOM outside the WebGL canvas.

questions.hint: ParticleContainer sacrifices complex hierarchy features for raw vertex streaming throughput.

questions.question: Why should dynamic 60 FPS numerical counters use PIXI.BitmapText rather than standard PIXI.Text?

choices.text: BitmapText creates no CPU canvas rasterization or GPU texture re-upload churn when strings change
choices.explanation: PIXI.Text generates a new offscreen HTML5 2D Canvas texture on every text change, creating VRAM churn and GC pauses. BitmapText merely batches pre-uploaded character glyphs.

choices.text: Standard PIXI.Text cannot render numbers
choices.explanation: PIXI.Text can render any Unicode text string.

choices.text: BitmapText runs on WebAudio instead of WebGL
choices.explanation: BitmapText is a WebGL display object.

choices.text: BitmapText automatically translates text into 12 languages
choices.explanation: Localization is an application-level concern.

questions.hint: Think about the memory and CPU cost of offscreen canvas rasterization.

questions.question: What is the optimal display strategy for a complex static vector UI background drawn with PIXI.Graphics?

choices.text: Redraw the entire vector path inside the 60 FPS Ticker loop
choices.explanation: Redrawing vector paths every frame causes unnecessary CPU triangulation overhead.

choices.text: Draw the paths once and bake them into a reusable Texture via app.renderer.generateTexture(graphics)
choices.explanation: Baking static vector geometry into a RenderTexture allows it to render as an ultra-fast batched sprite quad without recurring CPU triangulation.

choices.text: Convert the vector path into a raw HTML <video> tag
choices.explanation: Video tags are for video streams, not static vector shapes.

choices.text: Disable the GPU and use software rendering
choices.explanation: Software rendering is much slower than GPU acceleration.

questions.hint: Consider baking one-off vector drawings into a GPU texture.

props.title: The PixiJS Render Pipeline
paragraphs: PixiJS is built from the ground up to achieve desktop-class 60+ frames per second (FPS) rendering on the web. While traditional HTML5 Canvas API relies on synchronous CPU drawing commands that become bottlenecked when animating thousands of objects, PixiJS converts your scene graph into optimized GPU vertex buffers.
Understanding how PixiJS orchestrates coordinate spaces, batch rendering passes, and memory management is the key to creating fluid, stutter-free interactive applications.

At the heart of PixiJS is the **Display Tree**, rooted at `app.stage`. Every visible element in your application is a node in this tree. When an object moves, scales, or rotates, its transform is computed in two distinct phases:
**Local Transform**: The entity's position, rotation, scale, pivot, and skew relative to its immediate parent node.
**World Transform**: A $3 \times 3$ affine transformation matrix (`PIXI.Matrix`) representing the entity's absolute position, rotation, and scale relative to the root canvas coordinate space.
During the render loop, PixiJS performs a hierarchical depth-first traversal of the display tree. It multiplies each child's local transformation matrix by its parent's world matrix:
$$\text{WorldTransform}_{\text{child}} = \text{WorldTransform}_{\text{parent}} \times \text{LocalTransform}_{\text{child}}$$

This cascading matrix multiplication allows complex composite game objects — such as a character holding a weapon with its own attached particle emitter — to move, rotate, and scale effortlessly as a single unit without manual trigonometric calculations.

In WebGL and modern graphics APIs, the CPU communicating with the GPU via individual draw calls (e.g. `gl.drawElements()`) is the single most expensive operation. If an application draws 2,000 sprites with 2,000 individual draw calls, the CPU will spend most of its time in driver overhead, causing framerate drops and stutter.
PixiJS solves this with its internal **BatchRenderer**:

**Quad Geometry Buffering**: Instead of issuing a draw call for each sprite, PixiJS extracts the four transformed corner vertices of each sprite quad, its UV texture coordinates, vertex colors, and a texture unit index.
**Interleaved Buffer Packing**: Thousands of sprite quads are packed into a single continuous float buffer in system RAM and streamed directly to a single WebGL Vertex Buffer Object (VBO).

**Multi-Texture Binding**: PixiJS detects the maximum number of simultaneous texture samplers supported by the client GPU (typically 8 to 16 texture units). It binds multiple textures at once and passes the texture index as a vertex attribute, allowing sprites using different textures to render in the exact same draw call.
A batch break occurs when PixiJS is forced to flush its current geometry buffer and issue an immediate draw call before continuing. Batch breaks are triggered by:
**Exceeding Texture Unit Limits**: Referencing more unique BaseTextures in consecutive sprites than the GPU supports in a single draw pass.
**Blend Mode Switches**: Changing blend modes (e.g., from `NORMAL` to `ADD` or `MULTIPLY`).
**Custom Shaders and Filters**: Display objects with custom GLSL shaders or post-processing filters.
**Interleaved Vector Graphics**: Mixing un-batched `PIXI.Graphics` paths between standard sprites.
To maintain locked 60 FPS, high-performance applications group sprites by texture atlas and blend mode to minimize batch breaks.

WebGL applications run inside a sandboxed browser environment with finite Video RAM (VRAM). Unlike standard JavaScript objects, GPU textures and shader programs cannot be garbage-collected automatically by JavaScript engines like V8.
When you remove a display object from the scene tree (`parent.removeChild(sprite)`), the sprite's JavaScript wrapper may be cleaned up, but the underlying GPU texture buffer remains resident in VRAM.
To completely prevent memory leaks, you must explicitly destroy display objects and their associated texture assets:
```typescript
// Destroy sprite and its private GPU textures
sprite.destroy({
children: true,      // Recursively destroy all nested children
texture: true,       // Destroy the referenced Texture object
baseTexture: true,   // Free the raw WebGL GPU texture memory
When using shared texture atlases, set `baseTexture: false` so that destroying one sprite does not invalidate the shared texture atlas used by other active sprites.

scenarios.title: 2D Rendering & Asset Architecture Strategy
scenarios.description: Optimize rendering performance, memory footprint, and visual fidelity for a 2D web game running across mobile and desktop devices.

steps.title: 1. Asset Packaging & Texture Strategy
steps.description: Select how image assets, sprites, and animations are bundled and delivered to the GPU.

choices.label: Individual Loose PNG Images
choices.description: Load each character, prop, and particle as separate PNG image files on demand.

pros.title: Simple asset pipeline
pros.description: No sprite sheet build step required during development.

cons.title: Severe batch breaks
cons.description: Each distinct texture forces a separate GPU draw call.

cons.title: High HTTP overhead
cons.description: Dozens of network requests during initial scene load.

choices.whyThisFits: Quick prototypes with fewer than 50 sprites on screen.
choices.whenToUse: Early proof-of-concepts before asset pipeline automation.

choices.label: Packed Texture Atlas (Spritesheet)
choices.description: Pack all sprites, UI icons, and animations into unified 2048x2048 PNG/WebP atlases with JSON frames.

pros.title: Flawless batching
pros.description: Thousands of sprites render in a single GPU draw call.

pros.title: Optimized VRAM allocation
pros.description: Power-of-two GPU textures reduce memory fragmentation.

cons.title: Build pipeline step
cons.description: Requires TexturePacker or Spritesheet tool in build process.

choices.whyThisFits: Production games and high-performance interactive apps.
choices.whenToUse: Standard architecture for all production PixiJS applications.

steps.title: 2. Display Architecture for 10,000 Moving Entities
steps.description: Choose container primitives for managing bullets, particles, and background elements.

choices.label: Nested PIXI.Container Tree
choices.description: Organize all 10,000 entities inside standard nested Container nodes with full transform inheritance.

pros.title: Full feature set
pros.description: Supports individual masking, filters, and deep sub-nesting.

cons.title: Heavy CPU transform overhead
cons.description: Matrix multiplication for 10,000 nodes drops framerate on mobile CPUs.

choices.whyThisFits: Complex UI screens with deeply nested widgets.
choices.whenToUse: When objects need individual interactive children and masks.

choices.label: Flat PIXI.ParticleContainer
choices.description: Stream flat vertex buffers directly to the GPU using ParticleContainer with locked properties.

pros.title: Blazing 60+ FPS throughput
pros.description: Direct GPU buffer streaming handles 50,000+ sprites effortlessly.

cons.title: Restricted feature set
cons.description: No deep nesting, child masks, or individual child filters.

choices.whyThisFits: Particle systems, bullet hells, weather effects, and data visualizers.
choices.whenToUse: Whenever rendering thousands of flat, identical sprite instances.

choices.whenToUse: Headings, titles, and localized dialog strings loaded once.

choices.whenToUse: Any text that changes every frame or requires locked 60 FPS performance.

questions.question: Why should you pass `{ children: true, texture: true, baseTexture: true }` when destroying disposable temporary sprites?

choices.text: To ensure both the JavaScript DOM objects and the underlying WebGL VRAM texture allocations are freed immediately
choices.explanation: Without texture/baseTexture flags, GPU texture memory remains allocated on the graphics card even after JavaScript garbage collection sweeps the sprite.

choices.text: To restart the browser's GPU acceleration driver
choices.explanation: It manages application-level resource disposal without restarting drivers.

choices.text: To automatically reload higher-resolution textures
choices.explanation: Destroy completely disposes of the resource.

choices.text: To clear the browser's HTTP cache
choices.explanation: HTTP cache is distinct from WebGL GPU video memory.

questions.hint: Think about GPU memory leaks vs JavaScript CPU memory leaks.

questions.question: What is the primary performance drawback of applying post-processing Filters (like BlurFilter) to many individual sprites?

choices.text: Each filter pass renders the target into an offscreen framebuffer, forcing render target swaps and interrupting batch rendering
choices.explanation: Filters require offscreen render texture passes that break the batch renderer and incur GPU memory bandwidth costs.

choices.text: Filters delete sprite textures from disk
choices.explanation: Disk assets are unaffected.

choices.text: Filters disable all keyboard input listeners
choices.explanation: Input handling is unrelated to shader post-processing.

choices.text: Filters convert all 2D textures to 3D voxel models
choices.explanation: PixiJS remains a 2D rendering pipeline.

questions.hint: Consider the cost of switching WebGL framebuffers for offscreen render targets.
